questions.prompt: What is the purpose of professional API governance?
options: Replace testing with a one-time review meeting.
Treat retirement as complete before checking usage or communicating with consumers.
Make standards, ownership, inventory, change review, lifecycle decisions, and quality evidence explicit.
Prevent teams from documenting decisions so implementation can change silently.
questions.answer_key: Make standards, ownership, inventory, change review, lifecycle decisions, and quality evidence explicit.
questions.explanation: Make standards, ownership, inventory, change review, lifecycle decisions, and quality evidence explicit. This is especially relevant to “API Design Reviews” because the API contract must remain explicit and reviewable.

questions.prompt: For the lesson “API Design Reviews”, which check provides the strongest practical evidence?
options: Test against production records so the exercise cannot be repeated safely.
Review evidence, owners, risk acceptance, compatibility, operational readiness, and recovery.
Rely on a code review comment without running any representative check.
Run one happy-path call and skip invalid, denied, and failure scenarios.
questions.answer_key: Review evidence, owners, risk acceptance, compatibility, operational readiness, and recovery.
questions.explanation: A useful check is repeatable, tied to an observable contract, and includes an important negative or boundary scenario.

questions.prompt: Which review warning is most relevant to “API Design Reviews”?
options: No team owns the API contract, lifecycle, costs, or release evidence.
The expected behavior and relevant failure cases are documented.
A representative test can reproduce the result.
The API avoids exposing internal secrets and personal data.
questions.answer_key: No team owns the API contract, lifecycle, costs, or release evidence.
questions.explanation: This finding weakens a core API guarantee and should be treated as a design or release issue, not only a style concern.
